summary: The note is a Wikipedia article on avoidance coping, a psychological coping mechanism and form of experiential avoidance in which a person tries, consciously or unconsciously, to avoid dealing with a stressor. It covers links to substance abuse, social withdrawal, avoidant personality disorder, PTSD and depression, the approach versus avoidance coping distinction, how it is measured (MEAQ and BEAQ questionnaires, virtual reality), and treatments such as cognitive behavioral therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy. Navigation, citations and category boilerplate were ignored apart from the reference list context.
one_line: Avoidance coping is a psychological strategy of evading a stressor, linked to substance abuse, PTSD and avoidant personality disorder, and measured by experiential avoidance questionnaires.
key_facts: Avoidance coping is a coping mechanism and form of experiential avoidance characterized by a person's efforts, conscious or unconscious, to avoid dealing with a stressor.
Avoidance coping can lead to substance abuse, social withdrawal, and other forms of escapism.
High levels of avoidance behaviors may lead to a diagnosis of avoidant personality disorder, though not everyone who displays such behaviors meets the definition of this disorder.
Avoidance coping is a symptom of post-traumatic stress disorder and is related to symptoms of depression and anxiety.
Avoidance coping is part of the approach-avoidance conflict theory introduced by psychologist Kurt Lewin.
Literature on coping often classifies coping strategies into approach/active coping and avoidance/passive coping.

Traditionally, approach coping has been seen as the healthiest and most beneficial way to reduce stress, while avoidance coping has been associated with negative personality traits and poorer outcomes.
Avoidance coping can reduce stress when nothing can be done to address the stressor.
The Multidimensional Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire (MEAQ) was initially used to measure avoidance coping; it has 62 items rated on a scale of 1–6.
The Brief Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire (BEAQ) is used today and contains 15 of the original 62 items from the MEAQ.
In research, avoidance coping can be objectively quantified using immersive virtual reality.
Cognitive behavioral and psychoanalytic therapy are used to help those coping by avoidance acknowledge, comprehend, and express their emotions.
Acceptance and commitment therapy is a behavioral therapy that focuses on breaking down avoidance coping and is sometimes used to treat it.
Active-cognitive coping, such as changing one's attitude towards a stressful event and looking for positive impacts, is used as a replacement for avoidance coping.
Active-behavioral coping refers to taking positive actions after finding out more about the situation.
